title: cpu-side-bottlenecks-tokenization-request-parsing-threadpools-python-investigation
body:
Summary:

This doc captures a hands-on investigation into CPU-side bottlenecks observed during inference serving: primarily tokenization costs, request parsing/validation, thread-pool contention, and general Python runtime overhead (GIL, allocations, GC). Goal: quantify relative impact, propose mitigations with low risk and a prioritized experiment plan.

Context / motivation:
- Multiple customer-facing incidents reported increased p99 latency for short prompts (~16-128 tokens) even when model inference time is small.
- SLOs: 95th latency < 120ms for short requests; observed regressions to ~200-400ms under moderate QPS (50-200).
- Hypothesis: non-kernel work (tokenizer + JSON validation + Python per-request dispatch) dominates for short sequences and small outputs.

Environment / testbed:
- Serving runtime: v0.63.2 (local dev build with sampling instrumentation)
- Python: 3.11.4 (CPython) running uvicorn + gunicorn (uvloop) in pods
- Tokenizer: HuggingFace tokenizers (rust-backed where available), fallback to pure-python tokenizer for some models (legacy)
- Worker config: gunicorn: 4 workers, each worker spawns uvicorn with 2 threads for blocking threadpool (ThreadPoolExecutor)
- Hardware: c5.4xlarge-like instance (8 vCPU), representative of Dedicated small nodes used for PR testing
- Workload: synthetic load reflecting production: request size distribution: 60% short (<=64 tokens), 30% medium (65-512), 10% long (>512). Median output: 40 tokens. Burst QPS: 120.

Profiling methodology:
- High-level CPU sampling: py-spy record --native --output flame.svg (30s windows under steady-state QPS)
- Java/Native stacks: async-profiler for JVM-backed components (not used here, note for completeness)
- Linux perf (cycles, context-switches) for hotspot lines in C extensions
- eBPF off-cpu tracing (bcc/offcputime) to find blocking syscalls / thread scheduling delays
- Microbenchmarks: targeted functions measured with timeit and custom harnesses to isolate tokenization and JSON parsing
- Request path tracing: added lightweight per-request timers and histograms (tokenizer_ms, parse_ms, handler_ms, model_ms) in the console to validate profiler findings

Key findings (summary numbers are averages from repeated runs):
- Tokenization (HuggingFace tokenizer path) accounts for ~28-36% of CPU time for short requests. In setups that fell back to the pure-python tokenizer, it rose to 45-60%.
- Request parsing & validation (json.loads + pydantic model validation) accounted for ~12-18% of CPU time. pydantic v1 use amplified overhead; switching to pydantic v2 micro-bench gave ~2x improvement in validation speed in local tests.
- Thread pool queueing and worker dispatch overhead: measured tail latency introduced by the per-request blocking threadpool. Under 120 QPS with 4 worker processes and 2 threads each, queueing added ~15-40ms to p95 depending on arrival burstiness.
- Python interpreter overhead (GIL contention, allocations, GC): accounted for ~15-22% of observed CPU cycles. py-spy showed frequent short-lived allocations in request path (temporary dicts, list comprehensions in request normalization).
- JSON parsing library matters: switching from stdlib json -> orjson reduced parse time by ~30-40% and CPU percentage in the parsing stage accordingly.

Detailed observations:
1) Tokenization
- Rust-backed tokenizers (tokenizers crate used via HF Tokenizers) are consistently fast and show lower CPU %. However, we found a subset of models that still use Python fallback (legacy TTS/fragmented tokenizer code). Those fallbacks were the largest single contributor to excess CPU usage.
- Tokenizer warmup: creating tokenizer objects per-request (observed in an earlier PR) caused heavy allocations. Ensuring tokenizer is a long-lived cached object (one per process) removed repeated init costs and lowered CPU by ~6-10% overall.
- Batch tokenization: when requests are small, there is overhead per-call. Vectorizing tokenization for small batches (grouping 4-8 short requests) reduced per-request tokenization CPU by ~20% at the cost of added scheduling complexity and minor latency headroom.

2) Request parsing & validation
- Stdlib json.loads dominated parse time when incoming requests contained large metadata fields (traces, tool call params). Replacing with orjson reduced parse latency and CPU significantly.
- pydantic v1 validation was expensive for even shallow schemas. Moving to pydantic v2 or using dataclasses + orjson_deserialize for small schemas is a clear win.
- Extra work in user prompt normalization (regex, URL detection) contributed measurably; we found non-essential preprocessing steps that could be toggled off via request flags.

3) Thread pools and blocking work
- We found blocking disk or network calls occurring in the request path (credential fetch, KMS lookups on cold paths). These show up as off-CPU waits and increase effective threadpool queueing. Caching and asyncifying those calls eliminated the queueing in tests.
- Threadpool sizing: default ThreadPoolExecutor(4) per worker was too small under bursts. Increasing to 16 reduced queueing but increased context-switch overhead and marginally raised baseline CPU. Tradeoff: better p95/p99 latency vs slightly higher steady CPU.
- Gunicorn worker model: using multiple smaller workers (more processes, fewer threads) lowered GIL contention but increased memory footprint.

4) Python runtime overhead
- GIL contention shows up in py-spy as serialized CPU time across Python frames during high concurrency. For short, compute-light requests, the GIL mattered.
- GC pauses: saw a few 5-12ms stop-the-world pauses for large allocation bursts (mainly from tokenization fallback and request normalization). Tuning thresholds and enabling gzip-free object reuse helped.

Representative microbenchmarks (short request path)
- baseline: stdlib json + HF python tokenizer + pydantic v1: total pre-model CPU ~ 48ms per request (median)
- change 1: use HF rust tokenizer + tokenizer caching: pre-model CPU ~ 30ms per req (37% improvement)
- change 2: stdlib json -> orjson + pydantic v2: pre-model CPU ~ 22ms per req (54% improvement vs baseline)
- combined (rust tokenizer + orjson + pydantic v2 + cached tokenizer): pre-model CPU ~ 15-18ms per req -> shifted latency dominated by model inference as intended

Recommendations (prioritized):
P0 (low-risk, high-impact)
- Ensure tokenizer instances are process-scoped singletons (cache on startup). Add test to detect per-request tokenizer construction. Owner: Luca. (ETA 2d)
- Replace stdlib json.loads in hot path with orjson where possible (backwards compatible). Owner: Priya. (ETA 1d)
- Toggle off expensive prompt-normalization features by default; make them configurable per-route. Owner: Asha. (ETA 3d)

P1 (medium risk / coordinate cross-team)
- Migrate validation from pydantic v1 -> v2 in our request models. Create a compatibility layer for old schemas. Owner: infra + api. (ETA 2w)
- Increase threadpool sizes in controlled experiments and measure CPU vs tail latency tradeoff. Add autoscaling policy triggers based on threadpool queue depth. Owner: SRE. (ETA 1w)
- Introduce small-batch tokenization (vectorized) for short requests behind a feature flag. Measure latency impact on p50/p95. Owner: serving-runtime. (ETA 2w)

P2 (longer-term / higher effort)
- Move critical tokenizer codepaths into native extensions (C/Rust) if still using Python fallbacks. Owner: applied-ml + serving-runtime. (ETA 6-8w)
- Consider a fast-path C ABI for request parsing (binary protocol or compact protobuf) for internal high-volume customers. Owner: product + platform. (ETA Q2)

Experiments to run (concrete):
- A/B routing test: baseline vs orjson + pydantic v2 on 10% of traffic for 48h; measure p50/p95/p99, CPU/core, GC pause freq.
- Local perf run with threadpool tuning matrix: threads = {4,8,16,32} x workers={2,4} at 120 QPS to find knee point. Capture offcpu traces to ensure no blocking syscalls.
- Feature-flagged tokenizer caching + small-batch tokenization rollout to 5% traffic; measure per-request tokenization_ms and end-to-end latency.

Action items / TODOs:
- [ ] Add a CI check that warns if tokenizer object is constructed in request handler (Luca)
- [ ] Replace json.loads -> orjson in serving-runtime request dispatcher (Priya)
- [ ] Open RFC for pydantic migration (Ethan)
- [ ] Instrument threadpool queue depth metric and alert on > 50ms median queueing (SRE)

Notes / caveats:
- Some customers require request validation strictness that pydantic v2 may handle differently; plan a compatibility testing window.
- Microbenchmark improvements may not translate 1:1 in multi-tenant noisy shared nodes; sanity check in Dedicated staging cluster before opt-in.

Appendix: useful commands used during profiling
- py-spy (flamegraph): py-spy record -o flame.svg --native -- python -m run_load_test.py --qps 120 --dur 60
- orjson benchmark: python -m timeit -s "import orjson, json, data" "orjson.dumps(data)"
- check for per-request tokenizer construction: git grep -n "Tokenizer(" serving-runtime || run runtime analyzer
- off-CPU bpftrace snippet: sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_* /comm == "python"/ { @[comm] = count(); }'

References:
- Internal: RINF-2145 (incident), GH PR 789 (initial token-cache change), Confluence CPU Profiling Playbook

If reviewers agree with the prioritized list, next step is to schedule the P0 fixes into this sprint and begin the pydantic migration RFC.

Comments welcome — especially on any missed allocation hotspots or additional low-hanging wins we should try first.
